And if. See Taz and Magen Avraham, letter 4. Regarding fired bricks, specifically libun is required, while a brick dried in the sun has the law of an earthen utensil and is permitted through hagalah. If it was heated only from the outside, even after the fact it is forbidden, because its kashering follows its use: it absorbed chametz on the inside even though it was always heated from the outside. This is also the Gemara's rule regarding a baker's tile, which is heated outside and is forbidden. With metal utensils, filling them with coals must likewise be done on the inside. Heating them from outside, even if that is always their manner of use and they become so hot that sparks fly from them, is insufficient even after the fact. So is the Tur. See below. The same applies to a metal utensil for which hagalah suffices: if he inserted it into the boiling-water vessel only up to its rim and afterward treated the remaining portion, but the water did not reach the inner surface properly, it is forbidden even after the fact.

If hot beer was poured on the outside of an earthenware utensil and it absorbed the outermost layer, and he then returned it to our type of oven, even if we say, based on Pesachim 30b, that in such a case it is not repulsive because an outermost-layer absorption is easily expelled, and see Magen Avraham, letter 3, nevertheless it requires study after the fact, where this was done deliberately, whether food cooked in it on Pesach must be prohibited. Initially, Eliyah Rabbah, letter 3, already writes in the name of Issur VeHeter that the custom is not to rely even on returning it to the kiln. After the fact, or in a pressing situation when he has no other utensils, he may rely upon firing it again in a kiln.

For sometimes they use them, etc. In addition, pieces of bread are soaked in them for 24 hours, and something pickled for 24 hours is treated as cooked. [Hagahot Maimoniyot]

A heated stone. Bach writes that this does not have the status of an actual kli rishon and is effective only for jugs and cups. One should be stringent with bowls that have rims and protrusions like knobs and flowers, because it is impossible to pass the heated stone over every part of them. Such bowls therefore have no remedy except to insert them into a boiling-water vessel.

One should not prohibit after the fact. We do not say that a utensil necessarily carries its absorbed prohibition throughout its entire body, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, siman 121, seif 6, in Darchei Moshe. Issur VeHeter, Shaar 58, writes: the handle of a frying pan requires hagalah, though after the fact there is less concern. Certainly a wooden stirring spoon, which is ordinarily inserted entirely into the pot, requires hagalah. Even if one knows that only part was inserted, we rule that a utensil prohibited in part requires hagalah in its entirety. If part of a spoon was inserted into a prohibited food, he performed hagalah only on that part, and then inserted the spoon into a cooked dish, the dish is permitted, but the spoon must be kashered again by inserting all of it into boiling water. It appears to me that this is specifically where the part inserted into the cooked food was the part that had undergone hagalah. Even if the original prohibition spread through the entire spoon, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, siman 92, we do not say that it is expelled from the side that was not inserted, as stated in siman 94. If he inserted the side that was not kashered, however, the food is prohibited. This also appears from Yoreh De'ah, siman 92, seif 5, regarding a drop of milk that fell on a pot. Darchei Moshe's statement that the absorption does not travel through the whole utensil means that it does not necessarily emerge from the other side. In this way Beit Yosef's questions in Yoreh De'ah, siman 121, against Tur are resolved. Tur discusses a case where he wishes to use the portion he kashered, so kashering that portion is sufficient. If he wishes to use the other half, he must kasher that half as well. See there and the end of seif 26. What is written here, that we do not prohibit after the fact, means if he already used them. Initially, however, one may not use them even on Pesach where hagalah cannot now be performed.

By pouring. This too resembles pouring, because the absorption travels from this side to that side.

Before the fifth hour. This means before the beginning of the fifth hour, namely, by the end of the fourth hour, as stated above in siman 443. This is explicit in Tosafos and Rosh in Perek HaSocher Et HaPoel, in Perek Kol HaBasar, and in Perek Kol Sha'ah, as well as in Mordechai, Ran, and the other halachic authorities. This is also the reading in our copies of Tur, unlike some copies in which a scribal error reads "before the sixth hour." The later authorities agree, and the reason is clear: from the fifth hour chametz is at least rabbinically prohibited, so it is no longer considered a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. One must therefore ensure either that the water contains 60 times the utensil or that the utensil is not ben yomo.

Accordingly there is an apparent difficulty in Rama. Here he accepts the Mechaber's ruling without dispute, while at the end of the seif he writes that when one performs hagalah before Pesach after the sixth hour he must be careful about all these matters, implying that before the sixth hour he need not be careful. How can he rule leniently against the implication of most authorities? Taz and Magen Avraham already sensed part of this difficulty and left it requiring study. It cannot be answered that Rama means that from the sixth hour onward one must be careful even when the utensil is not ben yomo or there is 60, for according to the accepted halacha those factors remain relevant. The wording therefore requires careful interpretation.

The practical rule is that before the fifth hour, when the absorbed chametz is still permitted, several successive transfers of flavor may be treated leniently. From the fifth hour onward, however, one must observe the safeguards stated by the authorities. Where the utensils are ben yomo, the water must contain 60 against them; alternatively, the utensils must be allowed to remain unused for 24 hours. The utensils should be thoroughly cleaned before hagalah so that no tangible chametz remains upon them.

The water used for hagalah must remain boiling. One should not insert utensils one after another so rapidly that the boil ceases. If the water stopped boiling, one should wait until it boils again before inserting the next utensil. This is especially important for pots and utensils whose ordinary use is in a kli rishon. Bowls and spoons whose ordinary absorption is through pouring are more lenient, but one should nevertheless perform hagalah correctly.

A utensil should not remain in the hagalah water longer than necessary, because once it has expelled what it absorbed there is concern that it may reabsorb from the water. On the other hand, it must remain long enough for the boiling water to act upon it and cause the absorbed flavor to be expelled. Thus the language of Tur that one inserts and removes it "immediately" does not mean literally without any pause.

Utensils whose absorption is slight should preferably be kashered before utensils whose absorption is greater, so that the water remains cleaner of absorbed flavor. One should likewise ensure that the utensils are dry from cold water before immersion, so the hagalah water is not cooled.

Regarding the large vessel in which the hagalah is performed, the authorities discuss whether it must itself be kashered before and after the procedure. Where it is not ben yomo and hagalah is performed before the fifth hour, there is substantial basis to be lenient. Nevertheless, the custom is to kasher it at the beginning as a stringency. Some also require kashering it afterward, especially under circumstances where the water absorbed prohibited flavor.

The later authorities strongly criticize the common practice of conducting hagalah carelessly and rapidly without verifying that the water remains at a full boil. A Torah scholar knowledgeable in the laws of hagalah should ideally supervise the procedure. Sefer Chasidim, siman 730, writes likewise.

Rama's statement that "then chametz prohibits in the slightest amount" refers to Chol HaMoed. On Yom Tov itself hagalah may not be performed. When the prohibition of chametz has already taken effect, one must be careful with all the stated conditions, even where the utensil is not ben yomo and even where there is 60, in accordance with the stringent practices recorded by the later authorities.
